{{Short description|Concept in measure theory}}
{{More citations needed|date=May 2025}}
In [[measure theory]], given a [[Sigma-algebra|measurable space]] <math>(X, \Sigma)</math> and a [[signed measure]] <math>\mu</math> on it, a set <math>A \in \Sigma</math> is called a '''{{visible anchor|positive set}}''' for <math>\mu</math> if every <math>\Sigma</math>-measurable subset of <math>A</math> has nonnegative measure; that is, for every <math>E \subseteq A</math> that satisfies <math>E \in \Sigma,</math> <math>\mu(E) \geq 0</math> holds.<ref name="folland">{{cite book |last=Folland |first=Gerald B |author-link=Gerald Folland |date=1984 |title=Real Analysis |edition=1st |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |page=81 |isbn=0-471-80958-6}}</ref>

Similarly, a set <math>A \in \Sigma</math> is called a '''{{visible anchor|negative set}}''' for <math>\mu</math> if for every subset <math>E \subseteq A</math> satisfying <math>E \in \Sigma,</math> <math>\mu(E) \leq 0</math> holds.<ref name="folland" />

Intuitively, a measurable set <math>A</math> is positive (resp. negative) for <math>\mu</math> if <math>\mu</math> is nonnegative (resp. nonpositive) everywhere on <math>A.</math> Of course, if <math>\mu</math> is a [[Measure (mathematics)|nonnegative measure]], every element of <math>\Sigma</math> is a positive set for <math>\mu.</math>

In the light of [[Radon–Nikodym theorem]], if <math>\nu</math> is a σ-finite positive measure such that <math>|\mu| \ll \nu,</math> a set <math>A</math> is a positive set for <math>\mu</math> [[if and only if]] the Radon–Nikodym derivative <math>d\mu/d\nu</math> is nonnegative <math>\nu</math>-almost everywhere on <math>A.</math> Similarly, a negative set is a set where <math>d\mu/d\nu \leq 0</math> <math>\nu</math>-almost everywhere.

== Properties ==

It follows from the definition that every measurable subset of a positive or negative set is also positive or negative. Also, the union of a sequence of positive or negative sets is also positive or negative; more formally, if <math>A_1, A_2, \ldots</math> is a sequence of positive sets, then
<math display=block>\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n</math>
is also a positive set; the same is true if the word "positive" is replaced by "negative".

A set which is both positive and negative is a <math>\mu</math>-[[null set]], for if <math>E</math> is a measurable subset of a positive and negative set <math>A,</math> then both <math>\mu(E) \geq 0</math> and <math>\mu(E) \leq 0</math> must hold, and therefore, <math>\mu(E) = 0.</math>

== Hahn decomposition ==

The [[Hahn decomposition theorem]] states that for every measurable space <math>(X, \Sigma)</math> with a signed measure <math>\mu,</math> there is a [[Partition of a set|partition]] of <math>X</math> into a positive and a negative set; such a partition <math>(P, N)</math> is unique [[up to]] <math>\mu</math>-null sets, and is called a ''[[Hahn decomposition]]'' of the signed measure <math>\mu.</math><ref name="folland" />

Given a Hahn decomposition <math>(P, N)</math> of <math>X,</math> it is easy to show that <math>A \subseteq X</math> is a positive set if and only if <math>A</math> differs from a subset of <math>P</math> by a <math>\mu</math>-null set; equivalently, if <math>A \smallsetminus P</math> is <math>\mu</math>-null. The same is true for negative sets, if <math>N</math> is used instead of <math>P.</math>
